name: Dimethicone
summary: A silicone oil used as a skin protectant and hair-smoothing ingredient; trials cover medical uses, not appearance outcomes.
lead: Dimethicone, also known as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) or dimethylpolysiloxane, is a silicone polymer and a type of silicone oil. It ranges from a pourable liquid to a rubbery semi-solid depending on chain length, and it is hydrophobic and optically clear.

name: Shea butter
summary: A plant fat from African shea nuts used as an emollient; supported mainly by tradition and lab data, with no solo-ingredient appearance trials.
lead: Shea butter is a fat extracted from the nuts of the shea tree (Vitellaria paradoxa), which grows wild across the dry savanna belt of West and Central Africa. It is mainly a triglyceride fat rich in oleic and stearic acids, ivory in colour when unrefined.

name: Sodium PCA
summary: A skin-derived humectant salt used in moisturizers; safety is reviewed, but no appearance trials of the ingredient alone were found.
lead: Sodium PCA is the sodium salt of pyroglutamic acid (2-pyrrolidone-5-carboxylic acid, also called sodium pyroglutamate or sodium pidolate). It is used in cosmetics as a humectant, an ingredient that attracts and holds water, in dry-skin and hair products.

name: Sodium lactate
summary: A lactic acid salt used as a humectant and pH adjuster in personal care; its medical role is better documented than any appearance effect.
lead: Sodium lactate is the sodium salt of lactic acid (formula C3H5NaO3), a white powder or colourless liquid with a mild saline taste. It is made by fermenting a sugar source such as corn or beets and neutralising the resulting lactic acid.

name: Trehalose
summary: A protective sugar used in food, eye drops and some skincare; interest is in autophagy research, not proven appearance benefits.
lead: Trehalose is a non-reducing disaccharide made of two glucose units joined by an alpha,alpha-1,1 glycosidic bond. It occurs in bacteria, yeast, fungi, insects, invertebrates and plants but cannot be synthesised by vertebrates.

name: Polyglutamic acid
summary: A bacterial-fermentation humectant polymer marketed in skincare; real clinical use is as a drug carrier, not for appearance.
lead: Polyglutamic acid (PGA) is a polymer of the amino acid glutamic acid, existing as gamma-PGA (linked through the side-chain carboxyl) and alpha-PGA (linked through the alpha-carboxyl). Both forms are water-soluble and negatively charged.

name: Propanediol
summary: A glycol humectant and solvent that sits in the base of many skin products; it carries other actives rather than doing anything dramatic itself.
lead: Propanediol is the name for a small group of organic compounds with the formula C3H8O2 in which two hydroxyl groups sit on a three-carbon chain. Two isomers matter commercially: 1,2-propanediol, better known as propylene glycol, and 1,3-propanediol, which is often made by fermentation and sold in cosmetics as a plant-derived alternative.

name: Ectoin
summary: A bacteria-derived 'extremolyte' used in barrier and soothing skincare; lab data on UV stress exist, but appearance trials in healthy skin do not.
lead: Ectoin (also spelled ectoine) is a small, water-soluble amino acid derivative produced by many bacteria that live in salty or otherwise stressful environments. It acts as a 'compatible solute', protecting cells from osmotic stress, and has been commercialised as a cosmetic and medical-device ingredient for skin soothing, hydration and UV-related protection.

name: Beta-glucan
summary: An oat or yeast polysaccharide sold for soothing hydration; well studied as an immune-system trigger and dietary fibre, untested as a topical appearance treatment.
lead: Beta-glucans are a family of polysaccharides built from beta-linked glucose units, found in the cell walls of cereals such as oats and barley, yeasts, fungi, algae and some bacteria. Their structure, solubility and biological behaviour vary by source.

name: Allantoin
summary: A classic soothing and moisturising additive in drugstore skincare; used in scar and wound combination products, rarely tested on its own.
lead: Allantoin (5-ureidohydantoin) is a nitrogen-containing compound produced when uric acid is oxidised. Most mammals make it enzymatically; humans do not, and form only small amounts through reactions with reactive oxygen species. It is also found in plants such as comfrey, and cosmetic-grade allantoin is generally synthetic and described as chemically equivalent to the natural form.

name: Phytosphingosine
summary: A plant- and yeast-derived ceramide building block added to barrier and blemish skincare; cosmetic trials are not found in the sources reviewed.
lead: Phytosphingosine is an 18-carbon sphingoid base (2-aminooctadecane-1,3,4-triol) abundant in plants and fungi and also present in animals. It is a building block of more complex sphingolipids, including certain ceramides.

name: Cholesterol
summary: The body's key membrane sterol and a third of the skin's barrier lipid mix; in skincare it shows up alongside ceramides, with no appearance trials on its own.
lead: Cholesterol is the main sterol in animals: a structural component of cell membranes and a precursor to steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D. Nearly all animal cells can make it, with the liver and intestines producing about 80 percent of the daily total.

name: Squalene
summary: A skin-identical oil used as a lightweight emollient; safe-looking but with no trials for appearance outcomes.
lead: Squalene is an oily hydrocarbon (C30H50) and an intermediate in the biosynthesis of sterols such as cholesterol. It takes its name from Squalus, the shark genus whose liver oil was its first major source, and it is also made by the human body and secreted in skin sebum.

name: Natto gum
summary: A fermented-soybean polymer used as a humectant in face packs; documented in patents, not in trials.
lead: Natto gum is a cosmetic ingredient described as a sticky, water-soluble polymer produced by Bacillus bacteria during fermentation of soybeans, as in the Japanese food natto. It is associated with poly-gamma-glutamic acid (gamma-PGA), a water-soluble biodegradable polymer made from glutamic acid.

name: Lauric acid
summary: A coconut-derived fatty acid that mostly serves as soap and surfactant raw material; lab antibacterial data, no skin trials.
lead: Lauric acid (dodecanoic acid) is a saturated 12-carbon medium-chain fatty acid that makes up about half the fatty acids in coconut oil and palm kernel oil. It is used mainly to make soaps and surfactants for cosmetics and cleansers.

name: Panthenol
summary: Provitamin B5 humectant found in moisturisers and wound creams, with human data mainly for hydration and wound healing.
lead: Panthenol is the alcohol analogue of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5). It is converted in the body to pantothenic acid, so it acts as a provitamin; dexpanthenol is the biologically active D form, while cosmetics may use D-panthenol or a racemic DL mixture.

name: Jojoba oil
summary: A sebum-like liquid wax used as a moisturiser and carrier oil; popular, but with little trial data.
lead: Jojoba oil is a liquid wax pressed from the seeds of Simmondsia chinensis, a shrub native to southern Arizona, southern California and northwestern Mexico. About 97 percent of it is long-chain wax esters rather than triglycerides, making it unusually stable.

name: Tamanu oil
summary: A Pacific nut oil promoted for scars and acne; lab cell data exist, human trials do not.
lead: Tamanu oil is a viscous green-yellow oil pressed from the nuts of Calophyllum inophyllum, a tropical tree of the Indo-Pacific. It has been used in traditional medicine in Polynesia, India and Southeast Asia for wounds, burns and skin conditions.

name: Meadowfoam seed oil
summary: A very oxidation-stable plant oil from a Californian/Oregon wildflower, used as a cosmetic emollient with no published human skin-benefit trials.
lead: Meadowfoam seed oil is a vegetable oil obtained from the seeds of Limnanthes alba (white meadowfoam), an annual herb in the family Limnanthaceae native to wet grasslands, vernal pools and moist woodland in California and Oregon. The seeds contain roughly 20 to 30 percent oil, which is made up of more than 98 percent long-chain fatty acids.

name: Sea buckthorn oil
summary: A carotenoid-rich orange oil from Hippophae berries and seeds, used in creams and supplements, with small human trials but little skin-specific evidence.
lead: Sea buckthorn oil is a golden-orange to red oil obtained from the berries, seeds and sometimes leaves of the shrub Hippophae rhamnoides (now also classed as Elaeagnus rhamnoides), native to temperate Europe and Asia. Pulp oil and seed oil differ in composition: pulp oil is rich in palmitoleic acid and carotenoids, whereas seed oil is richer in linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids.

name: Evening primrose oil
summary: A gamma-linolenic acid-rich seed oil sold as a supplement and skin product; reviews find insufficient evidence for eczema or other conditions.
lead: Evening primrose oil (EPO) is a vegetable oil obtained from the seeds of the common evening primrose, Oenothera biennis, a North American plant that became naturalised across much of the world. The seeds contain about 24 percent oil, rich in the polyunsaturated fatty acids linoleic acid and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA).

name: Macadamia oil
summary: A palmitoleic- and oleic-rich nut oil used as a cosmetic emollient and cooking oil, with composition research but no clear human skin-appearance trials.
lead: Macadamia oil is a non-volatile oil pressed from the kernels of the macadamia tree, chiefly Macadamia integrifolia, a species native to Australia and now grown commercially. It is mostly monounsaturated: oleic acid is the main fatty acid, and palmitoleic acid, unusual in plant oils, is also present in notable amounts.

name: Grapeseed oil
summary: A linoleic-rich by-product of winemaking used as a light cosmetic and cooking oil, with no published trials on skin appearance.
lead: Grapeseed oil is a vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of grapes, a by-product of winemaking, with production concentrated in wine regions such as the Mediterranean. It is mostly linoleic acid (about 70 percent by one estimate) followed by oleic acid, with small amounts of vitamin E and plant sterols.

name: Black rice extract
summary: An anthocyanin-rich antioxidant extract from pigmented rice; lab and animal work is plentiful, but human skin evidence was not found.
lead: Black rice extract is a pigment-rich preparation obtained from the bran of dark-pigmented rice (Oryza sativa), whose colour comes mainly from anthocyanins. The grain is also called purple or forbidden rice; reference sources describe the "forbidden" label as a marketing term tied to claims of royal-only consumption.

name: Propolis
summary: Bee-resin K-beauty extract with lab antimicrobial data, little skin-specific human evidence and a known contact-allergy risk.
lead: Propolis, also called bee glue, is a sticky resinous mixture that honey bees make from plant exudates such as tree-bud resins and sap, combined with beeswax and saliva. Bees use it to seal gaps in the hive and to coat its interior surfaces . Its composition varies with the hive's location, season and local plants, and it typically includes flavonoids, phenolic acids and terpenoids .

name: Honey (topical)
summary: A moisture-drawing pantry staple with real wound-care data but no controlled evidence yet for skin brightening.
lead: Topical honey refers to honey applied to the skin, either as a home remedy and mask ingredient or as a processed ingredient in skincare. Honey is hygroscopic, meaning it draws in moisture, which is the basis for its use as a humectant . It also has a long folk use on burns and skin injuries .

name: Bee venom (topical)
summary: Korean 'faux-tox' bee-venom cream with no wrinkle trials found and an allergen-heavy ingredient.
lead: Topical bee venom is honey bee venom, or a purified or synthetic version of it, used in creams and masks marketed in Korean skincare as a natural 'faux-tox' alternative to botulinum toxin injections for wrinkles. Brand claims generally describe it as tightening or smoothing expression lines.

name: Galactomyces ferment filtrate
summary: Sake-yeast ferment behind brightening essences, with cell-lab data and product studies but few isolated human trials.
lead: Galactomyces ferment filtrate (GFF) is a cosmetic ingredient obtained from the fermentation of sake using Galactomyces yeast strains. It is marketed under trade names such as Pitera and is used in brightening and hydrating essences, especially in Japanese and Korean skincare .

name: Bifida ferment lysate
summary: Probiotic-derived ferment in repair serums, with lab barrier data and only combination-product trials.
lead: Bifida ferment lysate (BFL) is a cosmetic ingredient obtained by fermenting Bifidobacterium and then breaking down (lysing) the cells and extracting the result. It is used in repair and barrier serums as a 'probiotic' or postbiotic active .

name: Lactobacillus ferment
summary: Probiotic ferment in K-beauty creams with soothing claims, little skin-specific human evidence.
lead: Lactobacillus ferment (often listed on labels as Lactobacillus ferment or ferment lysate) is a cosmetic ingredient made by fermenting with Lactobacillus bacteria. It is used in K-beauty and 'probiotic skincare' products for barrier-support and soothing claims.
